The Petticoat Affair. Also known as the Eaton Affair. A social scandal that split President Andrew Jackson's Cabinet and exposed how fragile early-19th-century politics really were.

At the center was Peggy Timberlake Eaton. She was the widow of a Navy purser when she married Senator John Henry Eaton of Tennessee in 1829, just after Jackson had appointed Eaton as Secretary of War. And that's when Washington society turned on her.

The wives of Cabinet members, led by Floride Calhoun, the wife of Vice President John C. Calhoun, began spreading rumors about Peggy's moral character. They shunned her in public and insinuated she had been sexually immoral before her marriage. It was pure gossip, but it was relentless.

President Jackson took her side. He defended Peggy Eaton's virtue completely and demanded that all Cabinet families receive her socially. He was unflinching. People said his fierce protection came from what his own late wife Rachel had endured during Jackson's political career. Rachel had been attacked with similar rumors, and Jackson never forgot it.

This defense fractured his Cabinet. Secretary of State Martin Van Buren, a widower, sided with Jackson and actually cultivated Peggy Eaton's friendship. That move made Van Buren Jackson's favorite. But Vice President Calhoun and his allies weaponized the scandal. They used it to challenge Jackson's authority and force out anti-Jackson Cabinet members, particularly Secretary of the Treasury John Ingham.

By 1831, Eaton resigned as Secretary of War. The scandal had accomplished what Calhoun wanted. It contributed to the Cabinet's reorganization and poisoned the relationship between Jackson and Calhoun forever. What made it significant wasn't just the gossip itself. The affair exposed deep tensions about women's social authority, about how far a president could reach into private society, and about how brittle early political coalitions truly were.
